strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: cross-domain time-series forecasting with textual and visual side information, including both deterministic and probabilistic settings.
Presents an ambitious, coherent architecture combining modality-specific encoders, token distillation, modality-guided temporal attention, and prototype-conditioned flow matching.
Evaluation spans three benchmarks, multiple domains and horizons, and numerous established forecasting baselines; the reported aggregate improvements are often substantial.
Includes component ablations, inference-sampling analysis, computational-cost measurements, and relatively extensive per-dataset results.
weaknesses: The central multimodal claim is not adequately isolated. There is no clean ablation comparing time-only, time-plus-text, time-plus-image, and all-modality versions under identical pretraining and inference conditions. Existing ablations remove architectural modules rather than establish that either auxiliary modality supplies useful information.

There is a serious unresolved target-leakage concern in the synthetic corpus. GPT-4 receives raw time-series data and is explicitly asked to describe its 'future trend'; the paper never specifies whether the forecast target is hidden when generating each description. The example text itself describes detailed changes in the series. Test-time timestamp alignment and the information boundary for TimeMMD text are also unspecified.

The most important zero-shot multimodal results compare Aurora, which receives auxiliary modalities and extensive pretraining, primarily against unimodal foundation models. Meanwhile, the multimodal baselines are evaluated in a different supervised/few-shot comparison. This does not cleanly establish superiority over competitive multimodal or language-guided methods under matched information and training budgets.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a 418.6M-parameter model trained for roughly 30 days on eight A800 GPUs. The manuscript does not provide code, checkpoints, the generated corpus, complete prompts, generation model/version and filtering procedure, training duration in steps, modality-masking ratios, BERT/ViT variants and freezing policy, flow integration steps, or many optimization details.

The prototype-guided flow contribution is under-validated. There is no comparison against random learned prototypes, alternative conditional priors, standard flow matching with matched capacity, or other ODE solvers. Consequently, the results do not show whether the claimed period/trend initialization is responsible for gains rather than extra parameters or conditioning.

Results lack uncertainty estimates, multiple-run statistics, or significance tests. This is important because several claimed wins over Sundial are small, and Aurora is not uniformly best—for example, Sundial performs better on some deterministic and probabilistic aggregates.

Probabilistic evaluation is limited to CRPS and NMAE, with no calibration, coverage, sharpness, or qualitative distribution analysis. The predictive point statistic used for NMAE is not specified, and the reported improvement from increasing sample count may partly reflect Monte Carlo estimation rather than a better learned distribution.

Several technical and presentation details are imprecise: the FFT-period equation can be undefined if the dominant bin is zero and does not explain DC handling; attention-score scaling and dimensional projections are underspecified; some symbols are inconsistent; and Table 3's caption incorrectly refers to MSE/MAE. The paper also omits a limitations discussion and documentation of dataset licenses or potential issues in LLM-generated annotations.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and relatively underexplored problem: zero-shot multimodal time-series forecasting across domains.
Aurora combines modality-guided temporal attention with prototype-guided flow matching in a coherent end-to-end architecture.
The empirical study spans three benchmarks, deterministic and probabilistic forecasting, numerous baselines, and both multimodal and unimodal settings.
The paper includes component-level ablations, full per-horizon results, model-size information, and an inference-efficiency comparison.
weaknesses: The construction of the synthetic text raises a potentially fundamental target-leakage concern. The appendix says GPT-4 receives the raw time series and is prompted to analyze its future trend, and the resulting descriptions explicitly state trends. The paper never establishes that the forecast horizon is hidden from GPT-4. If target values informed the text, the central multimodal results would be invalid.

The comparisons are not adequately controlled. Zero-shot multimodal Aurora is compared mainly against unimodal foundation models, while the few-shot comparison contrasts a massively pretrained 418.6M-parameter model with fully supervised baselines. There is no compute-, parameter-, or information-matched multimodal baseline.

Reproducibility is poor: the exact pretraining series, source identifiers, temporal cutoffs, window-generation process, number of synthetic descriptions, GPT-4 version and decoding settings, contamination checks, training steps, random seeds, baseline hyperparameters, and checkpoint-selection protocol are not reported. No code, corpus, checkpoint, or release plan is provided.

The ablations do not substantiate the multimodal claims. Missing experiments include text-only versus image-only inputs, shuffled or irrelevant text, removal of synthetic descriptions, modality dropout rates, text-quality sensitivity, prototype initialization and bank-size ablations, and a conventional flow-matching decoder with otherwise matched capacity.

The probabilistic evaluation is insufficient. NMAE is a point-forecast metric, and the paper reports no calibration, interval coverage, sharpness, or likelihood-based measure. Figure 5 shows implausibly large improvements when increasing samples from 20 to 60, but offers no analysis or uncertainty, raising concerns about the sampling or metric implementation.

No confidence intervals, repeated-run variation, or significance tests are reported despite many small differences. Aurora is not consistently best—for example, Sundial is better on several deterministic and probabilistic averages—so claims that Aurora is the best-performing foundation model are overstated.

Important methodological details are underspecified, including whether BERT and ViT are frozen, how multi-head cross-attention scores are aggregated into the correlation matrix, how absent text is represented, how prototypes are initialized and trained, and how all losses and modalities are balanced during pretraining.

The claimed novelty is largely a composition of established elements—patching, RevIN, pretrained BERT/ViT encoders, cross-attention distillation, conditional transformers, and flow matching. The prototype-conditioned initialization is potentially interesting, but its advantage is neither theoretically characterized nor isolated through sufficiently controlled experiments.

The model is expensive: pretraining reportedly requires eight A800 GPUs for 30 days, while inference is slower than every listed baseline and compute is near the highest. This substantially limits accessibility and weakens the presentation of Aurora as an out-of-the-box tool.

Presentation quality is below top-tier standards, with frequent grammatical errors and typos, inconsistent metric descriptions, duplicated references, and broad claims unsupported by the reported evidence.

strengths: The paper presents a timely and meaningful contribution: a multimodal time-series foundation model supporting zero-shot, deterministic, and probabilistic forecasting. The reviewed manuscript is :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/a8ac001b2e0d4ecfba590cfdaae9f8a0/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

Aurora combines token distillation, modality-guided temporal attention, and prototype-guided flow matching in a coherent architecture. Conditioning the flow's initial state on learned trend and periodicity prototypes is intuitive and technically interesting.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: experiments cover multimodal and unimodal settings, zero-shot and few-shot inference, deterministic and probabilistic forecasting, three established benchmarks, and numerous strong foundation-model and supervised baselines.

Results are consistently competitive, with substantial improvements on several datasets. Component ablations support the usefulness of both modality-guided attention and prototype-guided flow matching, while the appendix provides full per-horizon results and an efficiency analysis.
The paper is generally well organized, and its central motivation—using external domain information to disambiguate similar histories that may have different futures—is compelling.
weaknesses: Evidence for the specifically multimodal claims is incomplete. The paper lacks separate text-only, image-only, no-modality, shuffled-text, corrupted-text, and modality-missing ablations. Consequently, it is unclear how much improvement comes from meaningful domain knowledge rather than model scale, pretraining data, or the endogenous image transformation.

The synthetic-text construction is underspecified and creates a potential leakage concern. GPT-4 receives raw time-series data and is explicitly asked to describe future trends, but the manuscript does not precisely state which portion of each series is exposed, whether forecast targets can enter the prompt, or how generated descriptions are filtered. This should be audited carefully for both pretraining and evaluation.

Comparison fairness is difficult to assess. Aurora has 418.6M parameters and requires approximately 30 days on eight A800 GPUs, yet there are no parameter-, data-, or compute-matched baselines. Several baseline entries are omitted because of pretraining overlap, making aggregate first-place counts imperfectly comparable.

Reproducibility remains limited: the exact corpus composition and sampling procedure, GPT-4 version and complete prompt templates, text-quality controls, baseline hyperparameters, random seeds, and uncertainty across runs are not reported. No code, checkpoints, or generated corpus release is stated.

The probabilistic evaluation reports CRPS and NMAE but does not examine calibration, coverage, sharpness, or sensitivity to the number of ODE integration steps. The unusually large performance change with sample count also deserves explanation and repeated-run uncertainty estimates.

The manuscript contains frequent grammatical errors and some overstated conclusions, such as calling Aurora the best-performing unimodal foundation model despite mixed dataset-level results and incomplete baseline coverage. It also lacks discussion of corpus licensing, LLM hallucinations, and possible harms when synthetic descriptions are used in health or security domains.

strengths: Ambitious and relevant problem: a single foundation model supporting multimodal, zero-shot, deterministic, and probabilistic time-series forecasting would be valuable.

The proposed system is technically coherent, combining modality-guided temporal attention with prototype-conditioned flow matching. The modality and component ablations generally support the usefulness of both components.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering five benchmarks, many domains and horizons, comparisons with numerous foundation and supervised models, and additional efficiency and qualitative analyses.
Aurora reports strong results in several settings, including substantial gains on multiple TimeMMD domains and competitive zero-shot performance on TSFM-Bench, ProbTS, and TFB.
weaknesses: The central multimodal evaluation has a potentially serious information-leakage ambiguity. GPT-4 is given raw time-series segments and reports and explicitly asked to describe the future trend; generated descriptions themselves state expected futures. The paper never establishes that the generator sees only information available at forecast time rather than target-window values. Without an auditable sample-construction protocol, the claimed cross-domain generalization gains are not reliable.

Comparisons do not cleanly isolate the contribution. Multimodal Aurora is compared against unimodal foundation models that lack its additional text input, while the multimodal competitors are mostly separately trained supervised models rather than comparable pretrained multimodal forecasters. Stronger controls using identical inputs, pretraining data, parameter budgets, and fine-tuning protocols are needed.

The pretraining corpus is insufficiently documented. The number of windows and paired descriptions, exact GPT-4 prompts and reports, temporal splitting, deduplication, overlap-detection procedure, text quality statistics, modality-masking rate, and cost are missing. Broad domain overlap between pretraining and evaluation further makes the unsupported claim of strict non-overlap especially important.

Reproducibility is weak despite the statement that everything can be reproduced: the code and checkpoint links are blank, and important training details such as training steps, scheduler parameters, random seeds, prompt templates, flow-integration step count, modality settings, and model-selection protocol are absent. Reproducing a 30-day run on eight A800 GPUs would also be prohibitively costly.

Results lack uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or significance testing. This matters because several reported advantages are very small, such as the TFB averages and a number of TSFM-Bench and ProbTS comparisons. Context length is selected separately for best performance, but the validation procedure is not specified, creating possible test-selection bias.

The probabilistic claims are supported mainly by sample-based CRPS and NMAE, without calibration, interval coverage, sharpness, or robustness analysis. It is also unclear whether the efficiency comparison includes the 100 samples used for evaluation, so the practical cost of probabilistic inference is not established.

Methodological novelty is moderate: BERT/ViT encoders, query-token distillation, cross-attention guidance, a learnable prototype bank, and conditional flow matching are largely established ingredients. Since the initialized period/trend prototypes become unconstrained learnable vectors, the claimed semantic interpretation and advantage over a learned conditional initialization require stronger evidence.

The manuscript overstates conclusions such as being the best-performing unimodal foundation model and a strong universal decision-intelligence tool. Performance is not uniformly best, baseline coverage is incomplete on several datasets, and ethical limitations of LLM-generated potentially hallucinated domain descriptions are not discussed.

strengths: The problem is important: external textual context can help disambiguate time-series histories that admit different future trajectories across domains.
Aurora presents a reasonably coherent architecture combining modality-specific encoders, modality-guided temporal attention, and conditional flow matching with learned prototypes.

The empirical study is broad, spanning multimodal, unimodal, deterministic, probabilistic, zero-shot, few-shot, and short-horizon settings. Modality and component ablations generally support the usefulness of the proposed modules.

weaknesses: The central “cross-domain” claim is not convincingly tested. Evaluation primarily measures transfer to held-out datasets whose domain categories—weather, energy, health, economy, and others—are already represented during pretraining; there is no explicit leave-one-domain-out experiment or systematic analysis on genuinely unseen domains.

The synthetic multimodal corpus raises a serious leakage and validity concern. GPT-4 is given raw time-series segments and explicitly asked to describe their “future trend,” but the paper never establishes whether the supplied segment excludes every prediction target. The exact segmentation procedure, prompts, temporal cutoffs, generated corpus, and contamination checks are not documented sufficiently to rule out target-derived descriptions. Moreover, LLM-generated summaries of the numerical series are a weak proxy for independently observed real-world modalities.

The comparisons do not isolate the effects of architecture, modalities, data scale, and compute. Aurora is a 210.8M-parameter model pretrained for roughly 30 days on eight A800 GPUs and over one billion points, while competing foundation models use different corpora, sizes, objectives, and availability exclusions. Main-table comparisons also mix Aurora at 10% adaptation with full-shot multimodal baselines. These results demonstrate competitiveness under heterogeneous conditions, not that the proposed mechanisms are responsible for state-of-the-art performance.

The prototype ablation is inadequate. Replacing the conditional learned prototype distribution with standard Gaussian noise simultaneously removes extra conditioning and capacity, so it does not establish that period/trend initialization is beneficial. Comparisons against conditional flow matching with a learned Gaussian mean, an equally parameterized initialization network, or alternative structured priors are missing. Because the prototype bank remains learnable, there is also no evidence that it retains the claimed periodic or trend semantics.

Probabilistic forecasting evidence is incomplete. CRPS is useful, but the paper provides no coverage, calibration, sharpness, reliability, or sample-diversity analysis. It also lacks repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, and significance testing, despite several reported differences being very small.

Reproducibility is poor. The code and checkpoint links in the reproducibility statement are blank, and important details—including the precise BERT/vision checkpoints, whether they are frozen, token counts, image resolution, masking probabilities, training duration in steps or epochs, scheduler parameters, sampling solver details, seeds, and corpus-generation artifacts—are absent. Reproducing the pretraining itself would also require unusually large compute.

The “first multimodal time-series foundation model,” “universal,” and strong out-of-the-box claims are overstated relative to the positioning and evidence. Closely related language- and vision-augmented forecasting systems already exist, while the paper does not sharply formalize what makes Aurora a foundation model beyond cross-dataset pretraining.

Presentation quality is below top-tier standards: the manuscript contains pervasive grammatical and typographical errors, incorrect or inconsistent citations, mislabeled metric captions, and imprecise terminology. These issues compound the ambiguity in the experimental protocol and technical description.

strengths: Aurora addresses an important and underexplored problem: zero-shot multimodal time-series forecasting. Combining textual domain knowledge, endogenous images, and time-series history in a foundation model is a clear and potentially impactful contribution.

The architecture contains several technically interesting components, particularly modality-guided temporal attention and prototype-guided flow matching. The conditional prototype initialization is well motivated and supports probabilistic forecasting.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, spanning five benchmarks and multimodal, unimodal, deterministic, probabilistic, zero-shot, few-shot, long-horizon, and short-term settings. Aurora obtains strong aggregate results against numerous recent foundation and supervised models.

The paper provides useful component ablations, full per-horizon results, corpus composition, model configuration, and computational-cost measurements. The comparable 10%-data experiments in the appendix further strengthen the evidence beyond the headline comparison with fully supervised models.
weaknesses: The construction of the central multimodal pretraining corpus is insufficiently controlled. GPT-4 receives raw time-series segments and is explicitly asked to describe future trends, but the paper does not state whether those segments include forecasting targets. This leaves a potentially serious target-leakage ambiguity. The exact GPT-4 version, complete prompts, generation parameters, corpus size in samples, rejection rate, and quantitative human-quality assessment are also missing.

Evidence for the specifically multimodal claims is incomplete. The ablations remove proposed modules but do not separately evaluate time-only, time+text, time+image, shuffled-text, irrelevant/noisy-text, or simple fusion alternatives. Consequently, it is unclear how much each modality contributes and whether the model genuinely uses domain semantics rather than correlations or LLM-generated trend labels.

Several headline comparisons are not fully like-for-like: multimodal Aurora is compared against unimodal zero-shot models that lack its additional information, while the main few-shot table compares 10%-trained Aurora against fully trained baselines. Fairer 10%-versus-10% results appear only in the appendix, and no simple pretrained text-conditioned baseline isolates the benefit of the proposed architecture.

The experiments report point estimates without repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Details about checkpoint selection and per-baseline context-length tuning are limited, making it difficult to judge whether relatively small gains on some datasets are robust.

Reproducibility remains incomplete because the displayed code and checkpoint links are blank and the generated multimodal corpus is not made concretely available in the manuscript. Reproducing pretraining also requires roughly 30 days on eight A800 GPUs.

The claimed universality and out-of-the-box practicality are somewhat overstated: evaluation remains focused on forecasting, realistic robustness to missing or misleading text is not tested, and Aurora has high inference cost—18.3G MACs and 83.5 ms in the reported comparison.
